title: Aramco Reopens the Taps to Europe and Russia Swaps Crude for Diesel
subhead: Saudi Arabia is offering discounted spot crude to European refiners it cut off three weeks ago, while Moscow's new diesel deal with Washington shifts Russian export flows from crude to refined product. Both moves show Gulf and Russian barrels re-routing around damaged infrastructure rather than returning to normal.

sections.heading: Aramco Offers Europe Discounted Crude Three Weeks After Cancelling October Volumes
sections.body:
Saudi Aramco is offering additional crude to European refiners for October and November loading, Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, just weeks after telling those same customers their October contracts would not be delivered following the attack that shut the East-West pipeline. Late-October spot cargoes were offered below official selling prices, loading either from Yanbu on the Red Sea or Sidi Kerir on Egypt's Mediterranean coast. November spot cargoes followed, and European buyers were told their full contracted November allocations would be honoured.

Saudi Arabia normally ships 700,000 to 800,000 bpd to Europe, much of it under long-term contracts. Traders told Bloomberg that the returning Saudi supply has already pushed down prices for some European crude grades this week.

The underlying recovery is real. The kingdom raised output by roughly one-third in September to more than 8 million bpd, rebounding from its lowest level in more than three decades in August. The IEA notes the UAE is at a record high and Iraqi exports are approaching pre-war levels.

What is notable is the pricing. Aramco is discounting into a market where the war premium is still intact — that is the behaviour of a seller that needs to re-establish customer relationships and prove its barrels can be delivered, not one maximising revenue on scarcity.
sections.whyItMatters: The East-West pipeline is back, but Saudi export credibility is not automatically back with it. Discounting spot cargoes is the price of convincing refiners to re-sign and re-schedule after a cancellation, and it tells you Riyadh expects the physical market to stay competitive rather than tight.

sections.heading: Russia's Diesel Deal With Washington Cuts Crude Exports Instead of Raising Revenue
sections.body:
Russia's crude exports from its western ports could fall by 100,000 to 200,000 bpd in November, according to preliminary loading schedules cited by Reuters and reported by Oilprice.com. The cause is not sanctions — it is the October 9 diesel agreement between Presidents Trump and Putin, under which refiners have ramped up processing, helped by units returning from maintenance, while Moscow issued new diesel export quotas and Washington eased sanctions on Russian fuel exports.

The arithmetic is awkward for Moscow. Higher refinery runs need more crude feedstock, and Russia has less of it: OPEC secondary-source estimates put September production at 8.64 million bpd, the lowest since mid-2020 and the tenth consecutive monthly decline. Moscow also cut its 2026 production forecast in September to a 17-year low. Seaborne crude exports already averaged 3.59 million bpd in the four weeks to October 18, down 110,000 bpd, with weekly flows at 3.13 million bpd — the lowest since March after a loading suspension at Primorsk. Novorossiysk loadings face delays of nearly three weeks as Black Sea shipping risks bite.

The trade is a clear win for Washington on paper: Russian diesel into a global fuel market where wholesale diesel has been pushed toward $200 a barrel, per Oilprice.com's earlier reporting, and where US pump prices have become a political problem before the midterms. It is a weaker deal for Russia, which is converting scarce crude into discounted refined product and losing crude export volume it cannot easily replace as Ukrainian strikes on refineries and Arctic navigation both wind down capacity.
sections.whyItMatters: The first real Western sanctions relief of this war is being spent on diesel, not crude. That tells you where the shortage actually is — and it means Russian crude availability to Asia, especially to China and India, tightens further just as both are competing for the same barrels.

sections.heading: OPEC+ Expected to Hold December Quotas With Production Still Below Target
sections.body:
The seven key OPEC+ producers — Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Kazakhstan, Algeria and Oman — are expected to keep quotas unchanged for December when they meet on Sunday, sources told Reuters. The group completed its phased rollback of 1.65 million bpd of cuts in September, but those targets have been largely nominal for eight months: Gulf producers slashed output in the spring as Hormuz flows collapsed.

Actual production continues to lag quota as the Iran war disrupted Gulf exports and the Ukraine war hit Russian and Kazakh flows. Attention inside the group has shifted to 2027 production baselines, which determine how individual quotas are calculated — the fight that will actually decide who carries the next round of cuts.

The interesting detail from Kpler data reported by Reuters' Ron Bousso and cited by Oilprice.com: October Middle East exports in total are higher than before the February strikes, with Hormuz flows averaging 11.7 million bpd, up from 9.8 million in September and close to February's pre-war 14.5 million. But that recovery is being bought with ship-to-ship transfers, record freight, and risk — and Kpler counted crude crossing the strait falling 27% in early October after a spike in attacks.
sections.whyItMatters: OPEC+ holding quotas while producing below them is a quiet admission that the group can no longer calibrate the market by decree. The 2027 baseline fight is where the real bargaining now happens.

sections.heading: Ras Tanura Fire Shows the Attack Campaign Is Now Aimed at Export Terminals, Not Just Fields
sections.body:
A fire broke out near Saudi Arabia's main Gulf export hub of Ras Tanura after an attack early Tuesday, and the kingdom said it contained it quickly, according to Bloomberg and reported by Oilprice.com. The extent of damage was not clear and it was not confirmed whether the hub itself was affected. Saudi Arabia said it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis toward the Eastern Region and four UAVs toward the Southern Region, per the official SPA agency.

The pattern this month is a widening target set. Fourteen people were killed in two missile strikes on Riyadh's international airport. Aramco's administrative building in Dhahran was hit two days later. Debris from intercepted drones killed two people near a processing plant at Shaybah, one of the kingdom's largest fields, though operations there were unaffected. On Monday the Houthis claimed attacks on pumping stations along the East-West pipeline — the Hormuz bypass — which Saudi Arabia has not confirmed. That pipeline was already down for two weeks in September after drone damage halted Yanbu loadings.

The escalation is tied to the Saudi-led coalition's push to retake parts of southwest Yemen that overlook the Bab el-Mandeb.
sections.whyItMatters: The attacks are no longer about taking out one facility. They are testing whether Saudi Arabia can keep both export corridors — Gulf and Red Sea — running at once. A simultaneous interruption of both would leave the kingdom with storage and discounts as its only tools, which is precisely the scenario its Singapore storage deal is built for.

sections.heading: India Says It Was Never Pressured on Russian Oil — and Is Buying Gulf Crude Anyway
sections.body:
Indian Oil Minister Hardeep Singh Puri said on Tuesday that the United States has not pressured India to cut Russian crude imports, telling Reuters he 'never felt anything' when asked directly. Puri framed the shift as pure economics: Indian refiners are buying more Middle Eastern crude because availability has risen and pricing is more favourable.

The trading data supports him. India's Middle East imports rose to 2.8 million bpd in September, up 32% from August and the highest since February, per Reuters vessel-tracking. Russian imports fell 14% to 1.8 million bpd, cutting Russia's share of India's crude slate from 46.6% to 33.5%, though Russia remained the single largest supplier. The mechanism is price: Urals loaded in the Baltic has risen to parity with Middle Eastern grades as China — deprived of Iranian barrels — competes for the same Russian supply.

Separately, Oilprice.com reports that India's fuel export earnings jumped 50% between April and September to $12.6 billion, driven by diesel and gasoline prices during the worst of the Middle East supply crunch. India has been one of the biggest commercial winners of a disruption it did not cause.
sections.whyItMatters: This is a useful correction to the standard story that Washington forced India off Russian crude. The switch was driven by relative price and Gulf availability recovering — which means it can reverse just as quickly if Urals discounts widen again or Hormuz flows stumble.

sections.heading: Rosatom Expands Bushehr and a $25 Billion Sirik Project While IAEA Access Stays Restricted
sections.body:
Russia and Iran are expanding nuclear cooperation, with Rosatom continuing construction on two additional Bushehr units and planning a $25 billion nuclear project at Sirik, according to RFE/RL reporting carried by Oilprice.com. Work on Bushehr's second unit is beyond 60% complete with a target of 2029 for start-up; a third is under construction. By October 11, Rosatom had 135 engineering and technical specialists back at the site after evacuating most workers when the US-Iran war began in February.

The legal frame is the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership Treaty that entered into force in October 2025, with an intergovernmental cooperation plan for 2024-2026 as the practical roadmap. The expansion comes as IAEA inspection access remains restricted and questions about Iran's enrichment programme are unresolved.

For Moscow this is commercial revenue plus a seat in Iran's long-term energy future. For Tehran it is technology, fuel, and expertise that no Western supplier will provide — and a civil nuclear programme that is harder to attack than an enrichment site.
sections.whyItMatters: Civil nuclear cooperation is how Russia embeds itself in Iran's energy system for decades regardless of how the war ends. It also complicates any future inspection regime: the more Russian-built and Russian-operated capacity exists, the more monitoring depends on Moscow's cooperation.

sections.heading: Dangote's $1.6 Billion IPO Closes Fully Covered, With Orders From 119 Countries
sections.body:
Nigeria's Dangote refinery reached its $1.6 billion fundraising target from domestic and retail investors alone, with total demand expected to significantly exceed even the $2.1 billion ceiling including the 30% over-allotment option, Bloomberg reported and Oilprice.com cited. Investors from 119 countries applied. The float values Africa's largest refinery at $47 billion and is the continent's biggest IPO.

The minimum subscription was set at just 10 shares, part of Aliko Dangote's pitch to reach 10 million retail investors. Proceeds go toward a $14 billion plan to double processing capacity from nearly 700,000 bpd to 1.4 million bpd by 2029.

The timing matters. This is a large refining complex coming online in the Atlantic Basin at the exact moment global product markets are short and diesel cracks are extreme. It is also African capital and African retail investors funding downstream capacity that has historically been supplied by European and Middle Eastern refineries.
sections.whyItMatters: A fully covered megaproject IPO in Lagos, with demand from 119 countries, is a signal that the market believes product shortages outlast the war. It also shifts pricing power in West African and Atlantic product trade away from importers toward a single Nigerian complex.

bottomLine: The day's pattern is infrastructure being patched faster than it is being fixed. Aramco is discounting spot cargoes to win back European refiners after cancelling October volumes; the East-West pipeline is running but was attacked again on Monday. Russia is converting scarce crude into diesel under a deal with Washington and will export less crude in November for it. OPEC+ will hold quotas on Sunday that its members cannot physically fill, and is already negotiating 2027 baselines. Meanwhile the Houthi campaign has moved from fields to export terminals and pipeline pumping stations, testing whether both Saudi corridors can be kept open at once. None of this is a return to normal — it is a system being held together with storage deals, discounts, and ship-to-ship transfers, and every one of those workarounds has a cost that shows up in price.
sources: Oilprice.com, Bloomberg, Reuters, SPA (Saudi Press Agency), Kpler, IEA, RFE/RL, Fox News, The Hill
